title: Induction, strong induction, well-ordering
summary: How to prove a statement for every integer: ordinary induction for sums, divisibility and inequalities, strong induction when a case depends on several earlier ones (postage, prime factorization, games, recurrences), and well-ordering (smallest counterexample) proofs. Induction proofs are near-certain on the final, and graders look for a labeled base case, a stated hypothesis and a correct step.

blocks.text: Induction proves a sum formula you already have; this section is about manipulating sums to find or use such formulas.
Σ<sub>k=m</sub><sup>n</sup> aₖ = aₘ + aₘ₊₁ + ⋯ + aₙ. k is the index (a dummy variable: any letter works), m the lower limit, n the upper limit. The sum has n − m + 1 terms.

blocks.name: Rules for manipulating sums
blocks.text: Σ (aₖ + bₖ) = Σ aₖ + Σ bₖ and Σ c·aₖ = c·Σ aₖ. Splitting: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> aₖ = Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>m</sup> aₖ + Σ<sub>k=m+1</sub><sup>n</sup> aₖ. Index shift: Σ<sub>k=m</sub><sup>n</sup> aₖ = Σ<sub>j=m−s</sub><sup>n−s</sup> aⱼ₊ₛ (substitute j = k − s and move both limits).
Σ aₖbₖ is not (Σ aₖ)(Σ bₖ), and Σ c = c·(number of terms), not c. Σk=110 3 = 30.

blocks.name: Geometric series
blocks.text: For r ≠ 1: Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>n</sup> a·rᵏ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1). For r = 1 the sum is (n + 1)a.

proof.text: Let S = Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>n</sup> a·rᵏ = a + ar + ⋯ + arⁿ.
Then rS = ar + ar² + ⋯ + arⁿ⁺¹ (the same sum shifted by one index).
Subtracting, every term except the ends cancels: rS − S = arⁿ⁺¹ − a.
So (r − 1)S = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1), and dividing by r − 1 ≠ 0 gives S = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1). ∎

blocks.name: Infinite geometric series
blocks.text: For |x| < 1: Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>∞</sup> xᵏ = 1/(1 − x).

proof.text: The partial sums are (1 − xⁿ⁺¹)/(1 − x). Since |x| < 1, xⁿ⁺¹ → 0 as n → ∞, so the partial sums tend to 1/(1 − x). ∎

blocks.text: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> k = n(n + 1)/2
Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> k² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> k³ = (n(n + 1)/2)²
Each closed form can be proved by induction (the standard sum-formula proofs); here you use them as tools to evaluate sums.

blocks.title: Change the lower limit
steps: Split: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>20</sup> k² = Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>3</sup> k² + Σ<sub>k=4</sub><sup>20</sup> k².
Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>3</sup> k² = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.

blocks.title: Index shift
steps: Substitute j = k − 2: when k = 3, j = 1; when k = 12, j = 10.
The sum becomes Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>10</sup> j² (still 10 terms).

blocks.title: A geometric sum
steps: This is geometric with a = 3, r = 2, n = 8 (9 terms).

blocks.title: Telescoping sum
steps: Partial fractions: 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1/k − 1/(k + 1).
Every middle term cancels with the next one; only the first and last survive.

blocks.title: A double sum
steps: Do the inner sum first, with i fixed: Σ<sub>j=1</sub><sup>3</sup> (2i − j) = 3·2i − (1 + 2 + 3) = 6i − 6.
Now the outer sum: Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>4</sup> (6i − 6) = 6·(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) − 4·6.

blocks.title: Infinite geometric series
steps: (b) Factor out the first term: Σ<sub>k=2</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1/2)ᵏ = (1/2)² Σ<sub>j=0</sub><sup>∞</sup> (1/2)ʲ (shift j = k − 2).

lesson.title: The principle of induction and sum formulas

blocks.text: To prove something for every n, prove it for the first n, then prove that being true for one n forces it to be true for the next.
A line of dominoes, one per n. If you knock over the first one, and every falling domino knocks over the next, then every domino falls: P(1) → P(2) → P(3) → ⋯
To prove P(n) for all n ≥ a: (1) base case: show P(a); (2) induction step: show that for every k ≥ a, P(k) → P(k + 1). Assuming P(k) inside the step is the induction hypothesis (IH).
Start anywhere: to prove P(n) for all n ≥ a, the base case is P(a) and the step is “for all k ≥ a, P(k) → P(k + 1).”
Clearly label both parts (“Base case”, “Induction step”) and state the induction hypothesis in words. Start with “By induction.”

By induction.
Base case (n = 1): check it directly.
Induction step: “Assume P(k): [write it out]. We need to show P(k + 1): [write out the goal].” Start from the k + 1 side, find the P(k) piece inside it, replace it using the IH, and simplify until you reach the goal. □

blocks.name: Sum of the first n integers

proof.text: By induction. Base case (n = 1): 1 = 1·2/2 ✓.
Induction step: let k ≥ 1 and assume 1 + ⋯ + k = k(k + 1)/2 (IH). We show 1 + ⋯ + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
So P(k) → P(k + 1) for every k ≥ 1, and by induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1. □

blocks.text: Picture proof: stack 1, 2, …, n dots as a staircase. Two staircases fit together into an n × (n + 1) rectangle, so twice the sum is n(n + 1). Notation: Σᵢ₌ₐᵇ f(i) = f(a) + f(a + 1) + ⋯ + f(b).

proof.text: Base case (n = 0): 1 = 2¹ − 1 ✓.

blocks.title: A sum formula proof
items: Name the claim. Write: “Let P(n) be the statement [the formula with n]. We prove P(n) for all n ≥ a by induction.”
Base case. “Base case (n = a): the left side is …, the right side is …, so P(a) is true.” Work out each side on its own and compare.
Inductive hypothesis. “Let k ≥ a be an integer and assume P(k): [the formula with k].” This is one fixed k, not every n.
Write the goal. “We must show P(k + 1): [the formula with k + 1 everywhere].” Now you know where you are heading.
Split off the last term. Start with only the left side of P(k + 1). Write it as (the sum up to k) + (term number k + 1). Get the new term by putting n = k + 1 into the general term.
Use the IH. Replace (the sum up to k) by the right side of P(k). Write “by the IH” on that line.
Simplify to the goal. Pull out the common factor (usually k + 1) and simplify until you get exactly the right side of P(k + 1).
Conclusion. “So P(k) → P(k + 1) for every k ≥ a. By induction, P(n) is true for all n ≥ a. □”

blocks.title: Sum of squares by induction
blocks.prompt: Prove 1² + 2² + ⋯ + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 for all n ≥ 1.
steps: Let P(n) be the formula. Base case (n = 1): left 1, right 1·2·3/6 = 1 ✓.
1² + ⋯ + k² + (k + 1)² — split off the new term (k + 1)², not k²
That is P(k + 1), so by induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1. □

lesson.title: Divisibility, inequalities and choosing the base case

blocks.name: A divisibility model proof
blocks.text: 3 | 4ⁿ − 1 for all n ≥ 1.

proof.text: Base case (n = 1): 4 − 1 = 3, and 3 | 3 ✓.

blocks.text: Key move: rewrite the k + 1 expression so the k expression shows up inside it.

blocks.title: Inequalities and where to start
blocks.prompt: Prove 2ⁿ > n for n ≥ 1, and 2ⁿ > n² for n ≥ 5.
steps: 2ⁿ > n: base n = 1: 2 > 1 ✓. Step: 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2·2ᵏ > 2k = k + k ≥ k + 1, using the IH and k ≥ 1.
2ⁿ > n²: the table gives n = 4: 16 = 16 (not >), n = 5: 32 > 25, so the base case is n = 5.
Step for k ≥ 5: 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2·2ᵏ > 2k² (IH).
2k² ≥ (k + 1)² ⟺ k² − 2k − 1 ≥ 0 ⟺ (k − 1)² ≥ 2, true for k ≥ 5 (indeed k ≥ 3).
So 2ᵏ⁺¹ > (k + 1)², and by induction 2ⁿ > n² for all n ≥ 5. □
blocks.answer: 2ⁿ > n for n ≥ 1; 2ⁿ > n² for n ≥ 5 (base case n = 5)

blocks.text: Harmonic numbers Hₙ = 1 + ½ + ⋯ + 1/n: one proves H₂ⁿ ≥ 1 + n/2 by induction. The step adds 2ᵏ terms, each at least 1/2ᵏ⁺¹, so it adds at least ½.
Inequality steps: use the IH once, then show the leftover inequality separately (often “k ≥ something”).

blocks.title: A divisibility proof
items: “Let P(n) be the statement d | f(n).” Base case: work out f(a) and show it equals d times an integer.
IH: “Assume d | f(k) for some k ≥ a, so f(k) = d·m for some integer m.” Naming m makes the algebra easy.
Goal: “We show d | f(k + 1).”
Make f(k) appear inside f(k + 1). Pull one factor out of each power: cᵏ⁺¹ = c·cᵏ. Then rearrange to get (number)·f(k) + (leftover).
Use the IH: replace f(k) by d·m. Check the leftover is a multiple of d.
Factor out d: f(k + 1) = d·(integer), so d | f(k + 1). Conclude as usual.

blocks.text: Shortcut for cⁿ − 1: cᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = c(cᵏ − 1) + (c − 1).

blocks.title: Divisibility with two powers
steps: Let P(n) be the statement 7 | 2ⁿ⁺² + 3²ⁿ⁺¹. Base case (n = 0): 2² + 3¹ = 4 + 3 = 7, and 7 | 7 ✓.
IH: assume 7 | 2ᵏ⁺² + 3²ᵏ⁺¹ for some k ≥ 0, so 2ᵏ⁺² + 3²ᵏ⁺¹ = 7m for an integer m. Goal: 7 | 2ᵏ⁺³ + 3²ᵏ⁺³.
2ᵏ⁺³ + 3²ᵏ⁺³ — the expression for n = k + 1, since (k + 1) + 2 = k + 3 and 2(k + 1) + 1 = 2k + 3
= 2·2ᵏ⁺² + 9·3²ᵏ⁺¹ — pull out one 2 and one 3² = 9 so the k pieces appear
= 2·2ᵏ⁺² + 2·3²ᵏ⁺¹ + 7·3²ᵏ⁺¹ — split 9 = 2 + 7 so both pieces get the same factor 2
= 2(2ᵏ⁺² + 3²ᵏ⁺¹) + 7·3²ᵏ⁺¹ — factor out the 2
= 2·7m + 7·3²ᵏ⁺¹ — by the IH
= 7(2m + 3²ᵏ⁺¹) — factor out 7; 2m + 3²ᵏ⁺¹ is an integer
So 7 | 2ᵏ⁺³ + 3²ᵏ⁺³, which is P(k + 1). By induction, P(n) holds for all n ≥ 0. □ The trick: split the big coefficient (9) into the small one (2) plus a multiple of 7.

blocks.title: An inequality proof
items: “Let P(n) be L(n) < R(n).” Base case: plug in n = a and compare the two numbers.
IH: “Assume L(k) < R(k) for some k ≥ a.”
Goal: “We show L(k + 1) < R(k + 1).”
Start from L(k + 1) only. Rewrite it so L(k) shows up, e.g. (k + 1)! = (k + 1)·k! or 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2·2ᵏ.
Use the IH once: swap L(k) for the bigger R(k). Now you have L(k + 1) < (something).
Close the gap: show (something) ≤ R(k + 1). This is a plain fact about k, and it usually needs k ≥ a. Say exactly where you use k ≥ a.
Write the chain: L(k + 1) < … ≤ R(k + 1). One strict < anywhere makes the whole chain strict.

blocks.title: An inequality that starts at n = 4
blocks.prompt: For which n is n! > 2ⁿ? Prove your answer.
steps: Table first: n = 1: 1 vs 2 ✗. n = 2: 2 vs 4 ✗. n = 3: 6 vs 8 ✗. n = 4: 24 vs 16 ✓. So we prove it for all n ≥ 4.
Let P(n) be n! > 2ⁿ. Base case (n = 4): 4! = 24 > 16 = 2⁴ ✓. IH: assume k! > 2ᵏ for some k ≥ 4. Goal: (k + 1)! > 2ᵏ⁺¹.
(k + 1)! = (k + 1)·k! — definition of factorial, so k! shows up
> (k + 1)·2ᵏ — by the IH, times the positive number k + 1
= 2ᵏ⁺¹ — exponent rule
So (k + 1)! > 2ᵏ⁺¹, which is P(k + 1). By induction, n! > 2ⁿ for all n ≥ 4. □ Notice the step works for any k ≥ 1. It is the base case that forces the start at 4: P(1) is false.

blocks.title: Choosing the base case n = a
items: The base case is the smallest n in the claim. “For all n ≥ 4” means base case n = 4, not n = 1.
If the problem asks “for which n is this true?”, make a table for n = 1, 2, 3, … first. Find the point after which it is always true. That point is a.
The IH is now “assume P(k) for some k ≥ a”, and you are allowed to use k ≥ a in the step (for example, k ≥ 4 gives k + 1 ≥ 2).
Test the step at the smallest k = a with real numbers. If the step needs a larger k to work, you need a larger a.

blocks.text: Strong induction lets you assume all earlier cases, not just the previous one. Well-ordering says every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element.
Base case(s): P(a) (or several: P(a), …, P(b)). Induction step: for every k ≥ b, [P(a) ∧ P(a + 1) ∧ ⋯ ∧ P(k)] → P(k + 1). You may use any earlier case, not just P(k).
Use it when the k + 1 case breaks into smaller pieces that aren't necessarily k.
Ordinary: “if I can reach rung k, I can reach rung k + 1.” Strong: “if I can reach every rung up to k, I can reach k + 1.” Sometimes you step up from a rung further down.

blocks.name: Existence of prime factorizations
blocks.text: Every integer n ≥ 2 is a prime or a product of primes.

proof.text: By strong induction. Base case (n = 2): 2 is prime.
Step: let k ≥ 2 and assume every j with 2 ≤ j ≤ k is a product of primes. If k + 1 is prime, done. Otherwise k + 1 = a·b with 2 ≤ a, b ≤ k.
By the IH (strong: a and b are smaller than k + 1 but need not equal k), a and b are products of primes, so a·b = k + 1 is too. □

blocks.name: Postage with 3¢ and 5¢ stamps
blocks.text: Every n ≥ 8 equals 5a + 3b for some integers a, b ≥ 0.

proof.text: Step: let k ≥ 10 and assume 8, …, k all work. Then k − 2 satisfies 8 ≤ k − 2 ≤ k, so k − 2 = 5a + 3b by the IH, and k + 1 = 5a + 3(b + 1). □

blocks.text: The step reaches back 3, so you need 3 base cases. Rule: the number of base cases = how far back the step reaches.

blocks.title: A strong induction proof
items: Name the claim. “Let P(n) be [statement]. We prove P(n) for all n ≥ a by strong induction.”
Base cases. “Base cases (n = a, a + 1, …, b): [check each one directly].” The next box tells you how many.
Inductive hypothesis. “Let k ≥ b and assume P(j) is true for every j with a ≤ j ≤ k.” Note k starts at b, the last base case.
Goal. “We show P(k + 1).”
Break k + 1 into smaller cases. Find smaller number(s) j, like k + 1 − 3, or factors of k + 1. Write one line showing a ≤ j ≤ k, so the IH covers j.
Use the IH on those j: “By the IH, P(j) is true, so …”.
Build P(k + 1) out of the smaller answers.
Conclusion. “By strong induction, P(n) holds for all n ≥ a. □”

blocks.title: Counting base cases
items: Write the step first. See how far back it reaches. If P(k + 1) uses P(k + 1 − s), the reach is s.
You need s base cases: P(a), P(a + 1), …, P(a + s − 1).
Why: for those n, n − s is below a, outside the claim. The step can't reach them, so you check them by hand.
The step then runs for k ≥ a + s − 1 (the last base case), so that k + 1 − s ≥ a.
If the step uses several earlier cases (like P(k) and P(k − 2)), count by the farthest one.
If the step uses “some smaller number” with no fixed distance (like factors or halves), one base case is usually enough. Just make sure every smaller number you use is still ≥ a.

blocks.text: Stamps rule of thumb: if the step adds one c-cent stamp, you need c base cases in a row.

blocks.title: 4¢ and 5¢ stamps, four base cases
blocks.prompt: Prove every amount n ≥ 12 cents can be made from 4¢ and 5¢ stamps: n = 4a + 5b with integers a, b ≥ 0.
steps: Let P(n) be “n = 4a + 5b for some integers a, b ≥ 0.” The step will take off one 4¢ stamp, so it reaches back 4: we need 4 base cases.
IH: let k ≥ 15 and assume P(j) for every 12 ≤ j ≤ k. Goal: P(k + 1).
(k + 1) − 4 = k − 3 — take one 4¢ stamp off
12 ≤ k − 3 ≤ k — k ≥ 15 gives k − 3 ≥ 12, so k − 3 is in the IH range
k − 3 = 4a + 5b with a, b ≥ 0 — by the IH (strong: P(k − 3), not P(k))
k + 1 = 4(a + 1) + 5b — put the 4¢ stamp back
a + 1 ≥ 0, b ≥ 0 — so this is a valid way to make k + 1: P(k + 1) ✓
By strong induction, every n ≥ 12 works. □ Is 12 the right start? Yes: 11 can't be made (with 0, 1 or 2 fives you need 11, 6 or 1 from fours, and none is a multiple of 4).
blocks.answer: Every n ≥ 12 is 4a + 5b (four base cases 12–15); 11 is not

blocks.title: Ordinary or strong?
items: If P(k + 1) follows from P(k) alone (sum formulas, one-step rules), use ordinary induction.
If k + 1 breaks into pieces that are smaller but not k (factors, halves, k + 1 − 3, two earlier terms), use strong induction.
Strong never hurts. If you're not sure, assume all earlier cases.

blocks.title: Strong induction for a game
blocks.prompt: A pile has n stones. Two players alternate removing 1, 2 or 3 stones; whoever takes the last stone wins. Prove the first player has a winning strategy exactly when 4 ∤ n.
steps: Let P(n): “the player to move wins iff 4 ∤ n.” Base case (n = 0): the player to move has no stones to take; the opponent took the last one, so the mover has lost, and 4 | 0 ✓.
IH: let k ≥ 0 and assume P(j) for all 0 ≤ j ≤ k. Goal: P(k + 1).
If 4 ∤ k + 1: write k + 1 = 4q + r with r ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Take r stones, leaving 4q ≤ k. By the IH the player to move from 4q loses, so the first player wins.
If 4 | k + 1: any move takes t ∈ {1, 2, 3}, leaving k + 1 − t, which is between 0 and k and not divisible by 4. By the IH the opponent (now to move) wins.
Both cases give P(k + 1). Strong induction was needed because the move jumps back 1, 2 or 3. □
blocks.answer: The first player wins iff 4 ∤ n (move to a multiple of 4)

blocks.title: Strong induction with two base cases
blocks.prompt: Let a₀ = 1, a₁ = 2 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2aₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2. Prove aₙ = 2ⁿ for all n ≥ 0.
steps: The step uses the two previous terms, so it reaches back 2: two base cases.
Base cases: a₀ = 1 = 2⁰ ✓, a₁ = 2 = 2¹ ✓.
IH: let k ≥ 1 and assume aⱼ = 2ʲ for all 0 ≤ j ≤ k. Goal: aₖ₊₁ = 2ᵏ⁺¹.
aₖ₊₁ = aₖ + 2aₖ₋₁ = 2ᵏ + 2·2ᵏ⁻¹ — IH at j = k and j = k − 1, both in range since k ≥ 1
= 2ᵏ + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ ✓. By strong induction aₙ = 2ⁿ for all n ≥ 0. □

blocks.title: A Fibonacci bound
blocks.prompt: With f₀ = 0, f₁ = 1, fₙ = fₙ₋₁ + fₙ₋₂, prove fₙ < 2ⁿ for all n ≥ 0.
steps: Base cases: f₀ = 0 < 1, f₁ = 1 < 2 ✓.
IH: assume fⱼ < 2ʲ for all 0 ≤ j ≤ k, where k ≥ 1.
fₖ₊₁ = fₖ + fₖ₋₁ < 2ᵏ + 2ᵏ⁻¹ < 2ᵏ + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹. □

blocks.name: Well-ordering principle
blocks.text: If A ⊆ ℕ is nonempty, then A has a smallest element.

proof.text: By contraposition: if A has no smallest element, show A is empty, i.e. a ∉ A for every a, by strong induction. Base case: 0 ∉ A (otherwise 0 would be the smallest). Step: assume 0, …, k ∉ A. If k + 1 ∈ A, it would be the smallest element. Contradiction!

blocks.text: Proof style it enables: “take the smallest counterexample (or smallest divisor, smallest element …) and show something smaller exists.”

blocks.name: Every n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor (well-ordering proof)
blocks.text: Every integer n ≥ 2 is divisible by some prime.

proof.text: Let D = {d ≥ 2 : d | n}. D is nonempty because n ∈ D. By the well-ordering principle D has a smallest element p.
Suppose p is not prime. Then p = ab with 2 ≤ a < p. Since a | p and p | n, a | n, so a ∈ D and a < p, contradicting the minimality of p.
So p is a prime dividing n. □

blocks.text: Induction follows from well-ordering: if P(n) failed somewhere, the set of counterexamples would have a smallest element m. m is not the base case, and P(m − 1) is true, so the step gives P(m), a contradiction.

blocks.name: Division algorithm (existence and uniqueness)
blocks.text: For d > 0 and a ≥ 0 there are unique q, r with a = qd + r and 0 ≤ r < d.

proof.text: Strong induction on a. If 0 ≤ a < d, the only option is q = 0, r = a.
If a ≥ d, then a = qd + r ⟺ a − d = (q − 1)d + r, and the IH gives a unique answer for the smaller number a − d ≥ 0. □

blocks.title: A well-ordering (smallest counterexample) proof
items: “Suppose, for contradiction, that P(n) is false for some n ≥ a.”
“Then the set C = {n ≥ a : P(n) is false} is a nonempty set of natural numbers.” (Nonempty because of step 1.)
“By the well-ordering principle, C has a smallest element m.” So P(m) is false, and P(j) is true for every a ≤ j < m.
If you need it, rule out m = a by checking P(a) directly.
Find a smaller element of C (a smaller counterexample), or use the true cases below m to show P(m) is true after all.
“This contradicts the choice of m as smallest. So C is empty, and P(n) holds for all n ≥ a. □”

blocks.text: Picture it: line up all the counterexamples. Grab the first one in line. Show someone is standing in front of it. That's impossible, so the line was empty.

blocks.title: Well-ordering: √2 is irrational
blocks.prompt: Prove √2 is not a fraction of positive integers.
steps: Suppose it is. Then C = {b ∈ ℤ⁺ : √2 = a/b for some positive integer a} is a nonempty set of positive integers. By well-ordering it has a smallest element b, with √2 = a/b, that is, a = √2·b.
1 < √2 < 2 — because 1 < 2 < 4
b < a < 2b — multiply by b, using a = √2·b
0 < a − b < b — subtract b from each part
√2 = (2b − a)/(a − b) — divide by a − b > 0; also 2b − a > 0 since a < 2b
a − b ∈ C and a − b < b — √2 is a fraction with the positive denominator a − b
So C has an element smaller than its smallest element b. Contradiction. So √2 is irrational. □ Pattern: assume a counterexample, take the smallest one, build a smaller one.
blocks.answer: √2 is irrational (a − b would be a smaller denominator)

blocks.title: Forcing the induction (strengthen the claim)
steps: Direct induction is stuck: knowing the sum is ≤ 2 says nothing about adding 1/(k + 1)².
Prove the stronger P(n): Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ 1/i² ≤ 2 − 1/n. Base n = 1: 1 ≤ 2 − 1 ✓.
Step: Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ⁺¹ 1/i² ≤ 2 − 1/k + 1/(k + 1)² (IH).
So the sum is ≤ 2 − 1/n ≤ 2. A stronger IH made the step easier.

lesson.title: Finding the flaw in a bogus induction

blocks.title: Spotting a broken proof
items: Base case: compute it yourself. Is it actually true?
IH: does it assume P(k) for one k (fine) or the claim for all n (circular)?
Direction: does the step start from P(k) and end at P(k + 1)? Or does it assume P(k + 1) and work backward to something true?
Algebra: check the new term and each line. A wrong next term is the most common slip.
Smallest k: run the step at k = a with actual small numbers. Many fake proofs fail only at the first step (like going from 1 to 2).
The first check that fails is the bug.

blocks.title: All horses are the same color?
blocks.prompt: “Claim: in every set of n ≥ 1 horses, all horses have the same color. Base n = 1: trivial. Step: given k + 1 horses, remove horse A; the other k are one color by the IH. Remove horse B instead; again the other k are one color. The two groups overlap, so all k + 1 have one color.” Find the flaw.
steps: Base case n = 1 is true.
The step is fine for k ≥ 2: the two groups of k share at least one horse, which ties the colors together.
Run the step at the smallest k = 1 (going from 1 horse to 2): removing A leaves {B}, removing B leaves {A}. The groups do not overlap.
So P(1) → P(2) fails, and every later step depends on it.
blocks.answer: The step from n = 1 to n = 2 fails: the two groups of size 1 do not overlap

blocks.title: Strong induction with a missing base case
blocks.prompt: “Claim: every n ≥ 1 equals 3a + 5b with a, b ≥ 0. Base: 3 = 3·1. Step: n = (n − 3) + 3 and n − 3 works by strong induction.” What is wrong?
steps: The step reaches back 3, so it needs 3 consecutive base cases.
It never checks 1, 2, 4, 7 — and in fact 1, 2, 4, 7 cannot be written as 3a + 5b.
Also n − 3 may be below the starting value, where the IH says nothing.
The true statement is: every n ≥ 8 is 3a + 5b (bases 8, 9, 10).
blocks.answer: Too few base cases: the claim is false for 1, 2, 4, 7; true for n ≥ 8

blocks.text: Assume P(k) and prove P(k + 1); never assume P(k + 1).
You must actually use the IH.
Make sure the step works for the smallest k. A classic fake proof that “x = y whenever max(x, y) = n” breaks because x − 1 or y − 1 can be 0, which isn’t a positive integer, so the IH doesn’t apply.
Wrong: “IH: assume P(n) is true for all n ≥ 1.” Right: “Assume P(k) for some fixed k ≥ 1.” (The first version assumes the whole theorem, so the proof goes in a circle.)

Wrong: writing the P(k + 1) equation, doing the same thing to both sides, reaching 0 = 0, and saying “true, so done.” Right: start with only the left side of P(k + 1) and turn it into the right side, one line at a time. (A true line can come from a false start: multiply 1 = 2 by 0 and you get 0 = 0.)

Wrong: for 1² + 2² + ⋯ + n², writing the k + 1 sum as (sum up to k) + k² or + (k² + 1). Right: the new term is the general term with n = k + 1, which is (k + 1)². (Plug k + 1 into the formula for the term; don't guess.)

Wrong: skipping the base case because “the step works.” Right: always check it. (Fake claim: n + 1 < n. The step k + 1 < k → k + 2 < k + 1 is perfectly valid, but the claim is false for every n. No first domino, nothing falls.)

Wrong: stopping at (k + 1)! > (k + 1)·2ᵏ and saying “so (k + 1)! > 2ᵏ⁺¹.” Right: add the missing link (k + 1)·2ᵏ ≥ 2·2ᵏ and say why (k + 1 ≥ 2). (Every link in an inequality chain needs its own reason.)
Wrong: in the 4¢/5¢ proof, checking only n = 12. Right: check 12, 13, 14 and 15. (The step for 13 would use 13 − 4 = 9, which is below 12 and not covered. Dominoes 13, 14, 15 never get pushed.)

Wrong: running the step “for all k ≥ 12” (the first base case). Right: “for all k ≥ 15” (the last base case). (At k = 12, k − 3 = 9 is outside the IH, so the step is not valid there. That's fine, because 13, 14, 15 are already base cases.)
Wrong: writing the IH as “assume P(k)” and then using P(k − 3). Right: “assume P(j) for all 12 ≤ j ≤ k.” (You can only use what you assumed. Say “strong induction” and assume every case up to k.)

Wrong: “take the smallest positive rational with property …” or “take the smallest counterexample” without saying why one exists. Right: use a set of natural numbers, and say it is nonempty because you assumed a counterexample. (The positive rationals have no smallest element: x/2 is always smaller.)

Wrong: in a factor argument, “k + 1 = a·b with a, b ≤ k” and allowing a = 1. Right: if k + 1 is not prime, then k + 1 = ab with 2 ≤ a, b ≤ k. (If a = 1, then b = k + 1 is not smaller, and the IH says nothing about it.)

cards.front: Prove 2 + 4 + ⋯ + 2n = n(n + 1) by induction.

back.text: Base case: 2 = 1·2. Induction step: k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2).

cards.front: Prove 5 | 6ⁿ − 1 for all n ≥ 1.

back.text: Base case: 5 | 5. Step: 5 | 6ᵏ − 1 by the IH, so 5 divides 6(6ᵏ − 1) + 5.

cards.front: What must every induction proof clearly contain?

back.text: A labeled base case, a labeled induction step, and the induction hypothesis stated in words.

cards.front: Prove every n ≥ 4 is 2a + 5b (a, b ≥ 0). How many base cases do you need?

back.text: Two base cases: 4 = 2·2 and 5 = 5. Step (k ≥ 5): k − 1 ≥ 4 works by the IH, so add a 2.

cards.front: Why does the 5a + 3b (n ≥ 8) proof need 3 base cases?

back.text: The step goes back 3 (from k + 1 to k − 2), so 8, 9, 10 must be checked directly.

cards.front: What's the least element of {n ∈ ℕ : n² > 50}?
What does “forcing the induction” mean?

back.text: Proving a stronger statement because its step is easier, e.g. Σ 1/i² ≤ 2 − 1/n instead of ≤ 2.

cards.front: Geometric series: finite sum formula and its proof idea?

back.text: Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>n</sup> a·rᵏ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1), r ≠ 1
Let S be the sum; rS − S telescopes to arⁿ⁺¹ − a. For |x| < 1, Σ<sub>k≥0</sub> xᵏ = 1/(1 − x).

cards.front: Closed forms for Σk, Σk², Σk³?

back.text: Σk³ = (n(n + 1)/2)²

cards.front: How do you shift the index of a sum, and how do you handle a lower limit other than 1?

back.text: Substitute j = k − s and move both limits by s; the number of terms n − m + 1 stays the same. For Σ<sub>k=m</sub><sup>n</sup>, compute Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> − Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>m−1</sup>, e.g. Σ<sub>k=4</sub><sup>20</sup> k² = 2870 − 14 = 2856.

cards.front: What is a telescoping sum?

back.text: A sum of differences Σ (bₖ − bₖ₊₁) in which consecutive terms cancel, leaving b₁ − bₙ₊₁. Example: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1 − 1/(n + 1).

cards.front: State the principle of mathematical induction.

back.text: If P(a) is true and P(k) → P(k + 1) for every k ≥ a, then P(n) is true for all n ≥ a.

cards.front: Template of an induction proof?

items: “By induction on n.”
Base case: check P(a) directly.
IH: “Let k ≥ a and assume P(k): …”
Goal: write out P(k + 1).
Start from one side of P(k + 1), use the IH, reach the other side.
Conclude: “By induction, P(n) for all n ≥ a.”

cards.front: Strong induction: what may you assume, and how many base cases?

back.text: Assume P(a), …, P(k) all hold. If the step uses P(k + 1 − s), you need s consecutive base cases, and the step runs for k ≥ the last base case.

cards.front: Well-ordering principle and the proof pattern it gives?

back.text: Every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has a least element. Pattern: assume a counterexample, take the smallest one, produce a smaller one — contradiction.

cards.front: Why does induction follow from well-ordering?

back.text: If P failed, the counterexamples would have a least element m > a; P(m − 1) holds, so the step forces P(m), a contradiction.

cards.front: When does ordinary induction get stuck but strong induction work?

back.text: When P(k + 1) depends on cases other than P(k): prime factorization (k + 1 = ab), postage (k + 1 − 3), recurrences using two earlier terms, games.

cards.front: Key move in a divisibility induction?

back.text: Rewrite f(k + 1) as (multiple of f(k)) + (obvious multiple of d), e.g. 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 4(4ᵏ − 1) + 3.

cards.front: How do you choose the base case for “for which n is the inequality true?”

back.text: Tabulate small n, find where it starts holding for good, use that as a, and check that the step works for every k ≥ a.

cards.front: What is “forcing the induction” (strengthening the hypothesis)?

back.text: Prove a stronger statement whose IH is strong enough for the step, e.g. Σ 1/i² ≤ 2 − 1/n instead of ≤ 2.

cards.front: The three classic bugs in a bogus induction?

items: the base case is false or missing
the step fails at the smallest k (horses: 1 → 2)
the step assumes P(k + 1) or uses an IH case outside the range

cards.front: Prove every n ≥ 2 is a product of primes.

back.text: Strong induction: 2 is prime. If k + 1 is not prime, k + 1 = ab with 2 ≤ a, b ≤ k; by the IH both factor into primes, so k + 1 does.

solution.text: Let an = 9n − 8n − 1. Basis: a0 = 0. Inductive step: assume 64 | an. Then
a<sub>n+1</sub> = 9·9<sup>n</sup> − 8n − 9 = 9(9<sup>n</sup> − 8n − 1) + 64n = 9a<sub>n</sub> + 64n
Both terms are multiples of 64. ∎ (Alternative: 9<sup>n</sup> = (1 + 8)<sup>n</sup> = 1 + 8n + Σ<sub>k≥2</sub> C(n,k)8<sup>k</sup>.)

Tests: writing an+1 as (multiple of an) + (obvious multiple of 64). Common mistake: expanding an+1 − an = 8·9n − 8 and then being stuck on whether 64 | 8(9n − 1). (It does, but that needs its own argument.)

hard.title: 3ⁿ ≥ n³ with four base cases

prompt.text: Prove 3n ≥ n³ for all integers n ≥ 0. (Watch which base cases you need.)

hard.answer: Proved: bases n = 0, 1, 2, 3; step for n ≥ 3 since (1 + 1/n)³ ≤ 64/27 < 3 (the step fails at n = 2).

solution.text: Step, for n ≥ 3: assume 3n ≥ n³. Then 3n+1 ≥ 3n³, and it suffices that 3n³ ≥ (n + 1)³, i.e. (1 + 1/n)³ ≤ 3. For n ≥ 3, (1 + 1/n)³ ≤ (4/3)³ = 64/27 < 3. ∎
The step fails at n = 2, since (3/2)³ = 3.375 > 3. So you cannot start the induction at 0 and go up one at a time: n = 0, 1, 2, 3 all need to be checked directly.
Tests: finding where the inductive step starts working and covering everything below it as base cases. Common mistake: using the step at n = 2 without noticing that it is false there.

hard.title: Postage with 5¢ and 8¢

prompt.text: Prove that every integer n ≥ 28 can be written as 5a + 8b with a, b ≥ 0. Show that 27 cannot.

hard.answer: Proved: bases 28–32, step n − 5; 27 is impossible (27, 19, 11, 3 not multiples of 5).

solution.text: Step: let n ≥ 33 and assume the claim for every k with 28 ≤ k < n. Then n − 5 ≥ 28, so n − 5 = 5a + 8b, and n = 5(a + 1) + 8b. ∎
27: 27 − 8b for b = 0, 1, 2, 3 gives 27, 19, 11, 3, none of which is divisible by 5.
Tests: strong induction with as many base cases as the step size (5). Common mistake: checking only 28 and stepping by 5, which leaves 29–32 uncovered.

hard.title: Σ 1/k² < 2 by strengthening

prompt.text: Prove Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> 1/k² < 2 for all n ≥ 1. (Trying to prove “< 2” directly by induction fails. Why?)

hard.answer: Prove the stronger Σ 1/k² ≤ 2 − 1/n; the step reduces to 1/(n+1)² ≤ 1/(n(n+1)).

solution.text: Knowing that the sum is < 2 says nothing about whether adding 1/(n + 1)² keeps it below 2. The hypothesis is too weak. So prove the stronger statement P(n): Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>n</sup> 1/k² ≤ 2 − 1/n.
Basis: 1 ≤ 2 − 1. Step: assume P(n). Then Σk=1n+1 ≤ 2 − 1/n + 1/(n+1)². We need this to be ≤ 2 − 1/(n+1), i.e. 1/(n+1)² ≤ 1/n − 1/(n+1) = 1/(n(n+1)), i.e. n ≤ n + 1. ✓
So the sum is ≤ 2 − 1/n < 2. ∎
Tests: when the induction is stuck, prove something stronger. Common mistake: writing “sum < 2, and 1/(n+1)² is tiny, so the new sum is < 2”.

hard.title: Three bogus inductions

prompt.text: Each induction proof below “proves” something false. Find the exact step that fails.

items: (a) Claim: any n ≥ 2 lines in the plane, no two parallel, pass through one common point. Proof: Two non-parallel lines meet. Assume it for n lines, and take n + 1 lines. Lines 1…n meet at a point P, and lines 2…n+1 meet at a point Q. Lines 2…n pass through both P and Q, and two distinct lines meet in at most one point, so P = Q.
(b) Claim: 2n = 0 for every n ≥ 0. Proof (strong induction): 2·0 = 0. Assume 2j = 0 for all 0 ≤ j ≤ k. Write k + 1 = a + b with 0 ≤ a, b ≤ k. Then 2(k + 1) = 2a + 2b = 0 + 0.
(c) Claim: n² + n is odd for all n ≥ 1. Proof: If k² + k is odd, then (k + 1)² + (k + 1) = (k² + k) + 2(k + 1) is odd + even, which is odd.

hard.answer: (a) step n = 2 → 3 fails (only one middle line) (b) step 0 → 1 fails (1 ≠ a + b with a, b ≤ 0) (c) no base case; 1² + 1 = 2 is even

items: (a) The step from n = 2 to n = 3 fails. The “middle” lines 2…n are then just line 2, a single line. One line contains both P and Q, so there is no second line to force P = Q. Every later step depends on this one, so the whole proof collapses.
(b) The step from k = 0 to k + 1 = 1 fails. You can’t write 1 = a + b with a, b ≤ 0. One of them would have to be 1, which is not ≤ k = 0.
(c) The step is fine, but there is no base case, and in fact 1² + 1 = 2 is even. (In fact n² + n = n(n + 1) is always even.)

solution.text: Tests: checking that the step works for the smallest k it is applied to, and that the base case exists. Common mistake: saying vaguely “the induction hypothesis is used wrongly” without naming the k where it breaks.

hard.title: Cutting a square into n squares

prompt.text: Prove that for every n ≥ 6, a square can be cut into exactly n smaller squares (they need not be the same size).

hard.answer: Proved for n ≥ 6: bases 6, 7, 8 and the step k → k + 3 (quarter one square).

solution.text: Bases.

items: 6: a 3×3 grid with one 2×2 block merged into a single square: 9 − 4 + 1 = 6.
7: a 2×2 grid with one quarter split into 4: 4 − 1 + 4 = 7.
8: a 4×4 grid with one 3×3 block merged: 16 − 9 + 1 = 8.

solution.text: Step. If a square can be cut into k squares, split any one of them into 4 quarters. That gives k + 3 squares. For n ≥ 9, the claim for n − 3 ≥ 6 holds by strong induction, so it holds for n. ∎
Tests: strong induction with step size 3, which needs 3 base cases. Common mistake: proving only the step “k ⇒ k + 3” from one base case, which covers 6, 9, 12, … but not 7 or 8.

hard.title: Zeckendorf-style Fibonacci sums

prompt.text: Let F1 = 1, F2 = 2 and Fk+1 = Fk + Fk−1 (so 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …). Prove that every positive integer is a sum of distinct terms of this sequence. Write 100 this way.

hard.answer: Proved by strong induction (greedy: subtract the largest term); 100 = 89 + 8 + 3.

solution.text: Strong induction on n. Basis: 1 = F1, 2 = F2, 3 = F3.

Step: let n ≥ 4 and assume the claim for all smaller positive integers. If n is itself a term, we are done. Otherwise pick k with Fk < n < Fk+1 (k ≥ 3). Let m = n − Fk. Then 0 < m < Fk+1 − Fk = Fk−1. By the hypothesis, m is a sum of distinct terms, each ≤ m < Fk−1 < Fk. So Fk is not among them, and n = Fk + (that sum) is a sum of distinct terms. ∎
Tests: greedy choice plus strong induction, and proving distinctness. Common mistake: forgetting to show that Fk isn’t already used in the representation of m.

hard.title: Shortest cycle in a tournament

prompt.text: A tournament is a directed graph in which every pair of distinct vertices has exactly one arrow between them. Prove that if a tournament has a directed cycle, it has a directed cycle of length 3.

hard.answer: Proved: a shortest directed cycle of length k ≥ 4 can be shortened via the v₁–v₃ arrow, so k = 3.

solution.text: The set of lengths of directed cycles is a nonempty set of positive integers. By well-ordering, pick a shortest cycle v<sub>1</sub> → v<sub>2</sub> → ⋯ → v<sub>k</sub> → v<sub>1</sub>. Here k ≥ 3, since there are no loops and no pair has arrows both ways. Suppose k ≥ 4. Look at the arrow between v<sub>1</sub> and v<sub>3</sub>:

items: If v<sub>3</sub> → v<sub>1</sub>, then v<sub>1</sub> → v<sub>2</sub> → v<sub>3</sub> → v<sub>1</sub> is a 3-cycle, shorter than k.
If v<sub>1</sub> → v<sub>3</sub>, then v<sub>1</sub> → v<sub>3</sub> → v<sub>4</sub> → ⋯ → v<sub>k</sub> → v<sub>1</sub> is a cycle of length k − 1.

solution.text: Either way we get a shorter cycle, contradicting minimality. So k = 3. ∎

Tests: the “shortest object” form of well-ordering. Common mistake: forgetting to explain why k ≥ 3 (tournaments have no loops and no 2-cycles), or not checking that the shortened sequence is still a genuine cycle. It is, because it uses a subset of the original distinct vertices.

hard.title: n-digit numbers of 1s and 2s divisible by 2ⁿ

prompt.text: Prove that for every n ≥ 1 there is an n-digit number, using only the digits 1 and 2, that is divisible by 2<sup>n</sup>. (The first ones are 2, 12, 112, 2112, 22112.)

hard.answer: Proved: prepend d ∈ {1, 2} with d·5ⁿ + m even; e.g. 2, 12, 112, 2112, 22112.

solution.text: Basis: n = 1, the number 2.
Step: suppose N has n digits, all 1 or 2, and N = 2nm. We put one more digit d ∈ {1, 2} in front: N′ = d·10n + N = 2n(d·5n + m). Then 2n+1 | N′ iff d·5n + m is even. Since 5n is odd:

items: if m is even, choose d = 2;
if m is odd, choose d = 1.

solution.text: N′ has n + 1 digits, all 1 or 2, and is divisible by 2<sup>n+1</sup>. ∎

Tests: an induction that builds the object, and the hypothesis has to carry the factorization N = 2nm. Common mistake: appending the digit at the end. That changes divisibility by powers of 2 unpredictably; putting it in front keeps N’s factor.

keyFacts: Geometric series: Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>n</sup> a·rᵏ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1) (r ≠ 1); Σ<sub>k≥0</sub> xᵏ = 1/(1 − x) for |x| < 1
Induction: P(a) and ∀k ≥ a (P(k) → P(k + 1)) ⇒ ∀n ≥ a P(n)
Always label the base case, state the IH for one fixed k, write the goal P(k + 1)
Divisibility: write f(k + 1) = c·f(k) + (multiple of d)
Inequalities: use the IH once, then close the gap with a fact about k ≥ a
Strong induction: assume P(a), …, P(k); step reaching back s needs s base cases
Well-ordering: every nonempty subset of ℕ has a least element (smallest counterexample proofs)
Bogus proofs usually fail at the base case or at the smallest k of the step

parsons.title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
parsons.goal: Prove by induction that 1 + 3 + 5 + ⋯ + (2n − 1) = n² for every integer n ≥ 1.
lines: Let P(n) be the statement 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2n − 1) = n².
Base case: for n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 1² = 1, so P(1) holds.
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 1 and assume 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2k − 1) = k².
Adding the next odd number, 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2k − 1) + (2k + 1) = k² + (2k + 1) by the inductive hypothesis.
k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)², which is the right side of P(k + 1).
So P(k) → P(k + 1) for every k ≥ 1, and by induction P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1.
distractors: Assume 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)² and simplify both sides until they agree.
Adding the next odd number, 1 + 3 + ⋯ + (2k − 1) + (2k − 1) = k² + 2k − 1.
Base case: for n = 2 we get 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², so P(1) and P(2) both hold.

parsons.title: 2ⁿ > n² for n ≥ 5
parsons.goal: Prove that 2ⁿ > n² for every integer n ≥ 5.
lines: Base case: n = 5 gives 2⁵ = 32 > 25 = 5².
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 5 and assume 2ᵏ > k².
Then 2ᵏ⁺¹ = 2 · 2ᵏ > 2k², by the inductive hypothesis.
It remains to compare 2k² with (k + 1)²: since k ≥ 5, k² − 2k − 1 = (k − 1)² − 2 ≥ 14 > 0, so 2k² = k² + k² > k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)².
So 2ᵏ⁺¹ > (k + 1)², which is P(k + 1); by induction 2ⁿ > n² for all n ≥ 5.
distractors: Base case: n = 1 gives 2 > 1, so the inequality starts at n = 1.
Since 2ᵏ > k², doubling both sides gives 2ᵏ⁺¹ > (k + 1)² immediately.
Assume 2ᵏ⁺¹ > (k + 1)² and divide both sides by 2 to get the inductive hypothesis.

parsons.title: 3 divides n³ + 2n
parsons.goal: Prove by induction that 3 | n³ + 2n for every integer n ≥ 0.
lines: Base case: n = 0 gives 0³ + 2·0 = 0, and 3 | 0.
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 0 and assume k³ + 2k = 3m for some integer m.
Regroup: this equals (k³ + 2k) + 3(k² + k + 1).
By the inductive hypothesis it equals 3m + 3(k² + k + 1) = 3(m + k² + k + 1).
So 3 | (k + 1)³ + 2(k + 1), and by induction 3 | n³ + 2n for all n ≥ 0.
distractors: Regroup: this equals (k³ + 2k) + 3k² + 3k + 1, and every term is a multiple of 3.
Since 3 | k³ + 2k, we get 3 | k³ and 3 | 2k separately.
Base case: n = 1 gives 1 + 2 = 3, and 3 | 3, which covers every n ≥ 0.

parsons.title: Postage with 4¢ and 5¢ stamps (strong induction)
parsons.goal: Prove that every integer n ≥ 12 can be written as n = 4a + 5b with integers a, b ≥ 0.
lines: Let P(n) say n = 4a + 5b for some integers a, b ≥ 0; we use strong induction on n ≥ 12.
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 15 and assume P(j) for every j with 12 ≤ j ≤ k.
Since k ≥ 15, the number k + 1 − 4 = k − 3 satisfies 12 ≤ k − 3 ≤ k.
By the inductive hypothesis, k − 3 = 4a + 5b with a, b ≥ 0.
Then k + 1 = 4(a + 1) + 5b, so P(k + 1) holds; by strong induction P(n) for all n ≥ 12.
distractors: Base case: 12 = 4·3 is enough, since every later value is reached by adding 4.
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 12 and assume P(j) for every j with 12 ≤ j ≤ k.
By the inductive hypothesis applied to k, k = 4a + 5b, so k + 1 = 4a + 5b + 1.

parsons.title: Every n ≥ 2 is a product of primes
parsons.goal: Prove by strong induction that every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of one or more primes.
lines: Base case: n = 2 is prime, so it is a product of one prime.
Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 2 and assume every integer j with 2 ≤ j ≤ k is a product of primes.
Case 1: if k + 1 is prime, it is a product of one prime.
Case 2: otherwise k + 1 is composite, so k + 1 = ab with 2 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ k.
By the inductive hypothesis, a and b are each products of primes.
Multiplying the two products writes k + 1 = ab as a product of primes; by strong induction the claim holds for all n ≥ 2.
distractors: Inductive hypothesis: let k ≥ 2 and assume only that k is a product of primes.
Case 2: otherwise k + 1 is composite, so k + 1 = ab with 1 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ k + 1.
By the inductive hypothesis applied to k, k + 1 = k · 1 is a product of primes.

parsons.title: Every n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor (well-ordering)
parsons.goal: Use the well-ordering principle to prove that every integer n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor.
lines: Suppose not; then the set S of integers n ≥ 2 with no prime divisor is nonempty.
By the well-ordering principle, S has a least element m.
m is not prime, since a prime would be a prime divisor of itself.
So m = ab with integers 1 < a < m and 1 < b < m.
Since 2 ≤ a < m and m is the least element of S, a ∉ S, so a has a prime divisor p.
Then p | a and a | m give p | m, contradicting m ∈ S; hence S is empty.
distractors: By the well-ordering principle, S has a largest element m.
Since a < m, a is prime, so a itself is a prime divisor of m.
So m = 1 · m, and 1 has no prime divisor, so 1 ∈ S, contradicting minimality.
